meta.title: Who wrote "Bitter Sweet Symphony"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: For over 20 years the credit — and the royalties — went to Mick Jagger and Keith Richards over a sample. In 2019 they signed the song back to The Verve's Richard Ashcroft. The full credit story.
meta.ogDescription: Written by Richard Ashcroft — but a sample dispute handed the credit to Jagger and Richards from 1997 until 2019, when they returned it.

writing.label: Written by Richard Ashcroft — credited to Jagger & Richards for 22 years
writing.sourceLine: The Verve’s 1997 hit was written by Richard Ashcroft — but it was built on a short sample of an orchestral recording of a Rolling Stones song, and a dispute over that sample handed the entire writing credit, and the royalties, to Mick Jagger and Keith Richards. They held it until 2019, when they gave it back.
writing.definitiveVersion: The Verve’s 1997 recording — the band’s signature song and one of the defining tracks of its era.
trail: ‘Bitter Sweet Symphony’ sampled a few seconds of an orchestral version of the Rolling Stones’ ‘The Last Time’, recorded by the Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra. The Verve licensed the sample from the recording’s owner (Decca) but, according to the Stones’ former manager Allen Klein and his company ABKCO, had not cleared the underlying composition.
In 1997 ABKCO prevailed: Jagger and Richards were awarded 100% of the publishing and royalties, and were credited as co-writers alongside Ashcroft — despite the song’s melody and words being his.

In 2019 Jagger and Richards agreed to sign the rights over to Ashcroft. Their manager confirmed future royalties would go to him, and that they no longer sought a writing credit — acknowledging, as far as they were concerned, that it is Richard Ashcroft’s song.

context.heading: When a sample rewrote the credit
lead: This is not a case of the public crediting the wrong person — it is one where the law, for two decades, credited the wrong people. Richard Ashcroft wrote the song; a dispute over a licensed sample transferred its authorship on paper to two musicians who had no hand in writing it.

We report the outcome rather than take a side on the original 1997 ruling: the writing credit and royalties were held by Jagger and Richards from 1997 to 2019, and were then voluntarily returned to Ashcroft. It is one of the clearest examples of songwriting credit being decided by rights law rather than by who wrote the song.
context.pull: For 22 years the law said two men wrote a song they hadn't written.

authors.name: Richard Ashcroft
authors.bio: The Verve’s singer and principal songwriter, who wrote ‘Bitter Sweet Symphony’. He lost the writing credit and royalties in a 1997 sample dispute and had them restored by Jagger and Richards in 2019.

authors.name: The Verve
authors.bio: The band whose 1997 recording of ‘Bitter Sweet Symphony’ became its defining hit.

schema.faqAnswer: "Bitter Sweet Symphony" was written by Richard Ashcroft of The Verve. Because it sampled an orchestral recording of a Rolling Stones song, a 1997 dispute credited Mick Jagger and Keith Richards as co-writers and gave them the royalties; in 2019 they returned the rights and credit to Ashcroft.
